phase1.explanation:
[[key:the storefront is open]]. Five units ago this started as a single blueprint — one class, one object — sitting in a workshop nobody outside could see. Here's the full arc, one more time, front to back.

[[term:Unit 1]] built the blueprint itself: syntax, variables, control flow, and the core idea that a class is a plan and an object is what you build from it. [[term:Unit 2]] extended that into families of blueprints — inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces — objects that share structure but specialize their own behavior. [[term:Unit 3]] was about trust: what happens when something in the workshop goes wrong, and how to catch, report, and recover from it instead of letting the whole operation crash. [[term:Unit 4]] stocked the shelves and hired help — Collections for organizing everything you'd built, Threads for getting more than one thing done at once.

[[term:Unit 5]] is the part where a customer, who has never once seen a line of your code, gets to walk up and use all of it. Stage and Scene gave the storefront a building and a window display. Layouts (VBox, HBox, GridPane, BorderPane) arranged the shelves. Controls stocked them with things a person could actually touch. Event handling made touching them mean something. CSS painted the shop. FXML let you redesign the window without touching the register's code underneath it. Binding put price tags that update themselves. ListView and TableView built the catalog board. Alerts gave the shop a voice for "are you sure?" Animation made the window display move. And the mini-app put every single piece of that under one roof, running.

[[fun:from here, the same core ideas keep showing up in bigger shapes]] — Spring Framework does dependency injection and web request handling on top of the same OOP fundamentals from Units 1–2; Android development uses its own View system that will look structurally familiar the moment you've built a JavaFX layout; enterprise Java leans hard on the same collections and generics you spent Unit 4 on. [[key:none of what you learned here was toolkit-specific — it was how software gets organized, and that transfers]].

phase2.explanation:
No broken code — one last conceptual lesson to close out the course. A few honest closing notes instead.

[[key:the fastest way to lose everything you just built is to stop using it]] — the next project you build, even a small one, is worth more than rereading these lessons a second time. Pick something slightly beyond your comfort zone and let yourself get stuck on it; that's where the real learning happens, not in a lesson that already knows the answer.

[[warn:Java keeps moving]] — new language features land roughly every six months since Java 9's release cadence began, and a few of them (records, pattern matching, virtual threads) will look unfamiliar even against everything in this course. That's normal — a solid OOP foundation is what lets you pick up each new feature quickly, not a reason to feel behind.

phase3.openingDialogue: One final question! What's next in your Java journey? 🤔

mcq.question:
What is the recommended framework for building web applications with Java?

A) JavaFX
B) Swing
C) Spring Framework
D) Android SDK

Select the CORRECT answer.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Java has shipped a new major version roughly every six months since Java 9 (2017)]] — a deliberate shift away from the old multi-year release cycle, specifically so new language features could reach developers faster instead of waiting years for the next big bundled release.
